introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 9 : dates de l'historiographie courante (Triple Alliance 1882, alliance franco-russe 1894 [convention militaire de 1892, ratifiée en 1894], Entente cordiale 1904, entente anglo-russe 1907, crises marocaines de 1905-06 et 1911, crise bosniaque 1908-09, guerres balkaniques 1912-13, attentat de Sarajevo le 28 juin 1914, « chèque en blanc » du 5-6 juillet, ultimatum du 23 juillet, déclaration de guerre à la Serbie le 28 juillet, guerre à la Russie le 1er août, à la France le 3 août, entrée en Belgique et en guerre de la Grande-Bretagne le 4 août 1914). Aucun chiffre de dépenses ni d'effectifs n'est avancé. L'énoncé suppose l'« inévitabilité » : le corrigé discute cette idée (les facteurs rendaient la guerre très probable, non strictement inévitable) sans modifier l'énoncé.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Analyse the factors which made the First World War inevitable by 1914.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The First World War broke out in the summer of 1914 after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. The question assumes that by 1914 the war was inevitable. It can be argued that a number of long-term factors, namely rival alliances, militarism and the arms race, imperial and economic rivalries, nationalism and Balkan instability, had created a situation in which a general war was extremely likely once a crisis broke out; but they made war highly probable rather than strictly unavoidable, since the actual decisions of governments in July 1914 still mattered.

**1. The alliance system.** Europe was divided into two armed camps. The Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy) dated from 1882; France, isolated by Bismarck, made an alliance with Russia (1892-94), and Britain ended its "splendid isolation" by the Entente Cordiale with France (1904) and the Anglo-Russian Entente (1907), which together formed the Triple Entente. As a result a local quarrel could involve all the great powers, and each power feared losing its allies and therefore supported them even in dangerous situations (as Germany supported Austria-Hungary and Russia supported Serbia).

**2. Militarism and the arms race.** The powers built large armies and war plans. After 1898 Germany's Navy Laws under Admiral Tirpitz led to an Anglo-German naval race, which worsened relations after the launch of HMS Dreadnought in 1906. Conscription, army expansion and detailed mobilisation schedules (the German Schlieffen Plan, which required a quick defeat of France through Belgium, and the Russian and French plans) meant that once mobilisation began it was hard to stop, and military leaders gained great influence over policy.

**3. Imperial and economic rivalry.** The competition for colonies and markets (Weltpolitik of Kaiser Wilhelm II, the Moroccan crises of 1905-06 and 1911 between Germany and France, the Anglo-German rivalry in trade and naval power, and Russian and Austrian ambitions in the Balkans) produced mistrust and a series of crises, in which Germany felt encircled by the Entente and the other powers feared German ambitions.

**4. Nationalism.** Nationalism was a major force. French revanchism over Alsace-Lorraine (lost in 1871), Pan-Germanism, Pan-Slavism (Russia's protection of the Slavs) and the national ambitions of Serbs, Czechs, South Slavs and others threatened the multinational Austria-Hungary, which regarded Serbia as a danger to its survival. Public opinion and the press often encouraged aggressive attitudes.

**5. The Balkan crises.** The decline of the Ottoman Empire left a power vacuum in the Balkans. Austria's annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1908 angered Serbia and Russia; the Balkan Wars of 1912-13 increased Serbian strength and Austrian fears. Russia, humiliated in 1908, was determined not to abandon Serbia again, and Germany was determined to support its ally.

**6. The July Crisis of 1914.** Franz Ferdinand was killed by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist linked to groups supported from Serbia. On 5-6 July Germany gave Austria-Hungary unconditional support (the "blank cheque"), and on 23 July Austria presented Serbia with a harsh ultimatum; the Serbian reply was not accepted and Austria declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Russia mobilised in support of Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, and Germany invaded Belgium; Britain, bound by the Treaty of London of 1839 to defend Belgian neutrality and concerned about the balance of power, declared war on Germany on 4 August.

**7. Was the war really inevitable?** Several earlier crises (Morocco, Bosnia, the Balkan Wars) had been settled without a general war, and in 1912-14 Anglo-German relations had improved a little; the actions of statesmen in July 1914, including German willingness to risk a continental war and Austria's decision to punish Serbia, were decisive. Historians such as Fritz Fischer have stressed German aims and responsibility, while others point to the shared responsibility of all the powers. However, the combination of the alliance system, military plans and the nationalist tension in the Balkans meant that any serious crisis was likely to escalate.

**Conclusion.** By 1914 the alliance system, the arms race and rigid mobilisation plans, imperial rivalries, nationalism and Balkan instability had created conditions in which a European war was highly probable. The assassination at Sarajevo and the decisions of the governments in July 1914 turned this probability into reality, so that the war was the product of deep-rooted causes together with human choices rather than the result of a fate that could not have been avoided.
